summary: Builds representational fluency between a partitioned rectangle (area model) and the distributive equation a×(b+c) = a×b + a×c. The same picture that shows 6×13 = 6×10 + 6×3 later underwrites partial products and long multiplication. Rests on spatial structuring (seeing a region as rows and columns) and on area being additive, both built earlier. Learners should translate BOTH ways — read a model into an equation and draw a model for an equation — and keep the repeated factor visible on both sub-rectangles.
misconceptions: Distributes to only one addend: 6×(10+3) = 6×10 + 3 (drops the ×6 on the second part)
Adds the side lengths instead of the region areas (6 + 13, or 10 + 3)
Cannot place the split so the two parts recompose to the whole — a spatial-structuring difficulty
Computes the two sub-areas but forgets to add them into the whole

activities.title: Cut the rectangle, keep the factor
steps: Tile a 3×(4+2) rectangle (3 rows of 6 tiles), then physically cut it along the grid line between the first 4 columns and the last 2 columns, making two sub-rectangles.
Match each piece to its product (3×4 and 3×2) and match the whole uncut rectangle to 3×(4+2).
Say out loud how tall BOTH pieces are (still 3 rows), confirming the repeated factor appears on each part.
Recompose the pieces and check the two areas sum to the whole.
activities.insight: A rectangle a×(b+c) split by one line across its (b+c) side, at the point between b and c, becomes two sub-rectangles a×b and a×c whose areas SUM to the whole; the repeated factor 'a' stays on both parts.

activities.title: Split at the ten to make a hard fact easy
steps: On a 6-by-13 rectangle on a grid, place one vertical split line under the '10'.
Label the two regions with their products (6×10 = 60 and 6×3 = 18) and write the matching equation 6×13 = 6×10 + 6×3 = 78 beside the picture.
Once comfortable, re-label the same partition as an open array — mark each region by its dimensions (6×10 and 6×3) without drawing every tile — as a step toward purely symbolic partial products.
Try a different split of the same rectangle (e.g. 6×7 and 6×6) and check the total is still 78.
Explain why splitting at the ten makes the calculation easier even though any valid split gives the same total.
activities.insight: Splitting at a friendly number (the ten) turns a hard product into two known facts; the split is a strategy the learner chooses, and different valid splits all recompose to the same total (additivity).

activities.title: Read it and draw it both ways
steps: Given a rectangle split into a shaded 6×10 region and a 6×3 region, state the multiplication each shaded part stands for and what they make together.
Given 5×12, draw your own area model, choose where to split it, and write the matching equation (e.g. splitting at the ten: 5×12 = 5×10 + 5×2 = 50 + 10 = 60).
Keep the factor 5 on BOTH sub-rectangles and recompose to the whole.
Examine a worked example such as '6×13 = 6×10 + 3', find the error, and say what was forgotten.
activities.insight: Fluency means moving in both directions: reading a given model into an equation AND constructing a model for a given equation, keeping the common factor and recomposing to the whole.

activities.title: Reveal the parts, then the whole
steps: On a static split area model of 6×13, reveal the left region's product (6×10 = 60), then the right region's (6×3 = 18).
Reveal the whole rectangle's value (6×13 = 78) and state in words that it is the two parts added.
Re-tell the chain: two parts → added → whole.
activities.insight: The whole area equals the sum of the two sub-areas; revealing them in sequence makes the 'add the parts' step explicit.

checkQuestion: Show an area model of 6 × 13: a rectangle split by one line into a shaded 6×10 region and a differently-shaded 6×3 region. FIRST (interpret): 'This picture shows 6 × 13. Point to the two parts — what multiplication does each shaded part stand for, and what happens when you put them together?' THEN (translate/produce): 'Now here is 5 × 12. Draw an area model that splits it to make it easier to work out, and write the matching equation.'
checkAnswer: Interpret: the left region is 6×10 = 60, the right is 6×3 = 18, and together they are the whole rectangle, so 6×13 = 6×10 + 6×3 = 78. Produce: draws a 5×12 rectangle split into 5×10 and 5×2, writes 5×12 = 5×10 + 5×2 = 50 + 10 = 60, with the split at the ten and the factor 5 kept on BOTH sub-rectangles.
